authoritative

/uh-THOR-ih-tay-tiv/ - the stress falls on THOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Authoritative means commanding trust and deference as expert, accurate, and reliable.

Field guides come and go, but Merrick's remains the authoritative one: when two rangers disagree about a track, someone reaches for 'the Merrick' and the argument ends.

Example

Two accounts of the mine disaster appeared within a year. A journalist's version sold better, but the inspector's report became the authoritative account: she had descended the shaft herself, logged every timber and valve, and taken sworn statements from all forty-one survivors. Courts cited her; eventually, the journalist cited her too.

Authoritative marks the version others defer to and build on, because expertise and evidence stand behind it. Note what it does not mean: the inspector held power over no one. An authoritative voice is obeyed the way a good map is obeyed — willingly, because doubting it costs more than trusting it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

definitive: Definitive means the question is settled: the last word, after which debate stops. Authoritative is about weight rather than finality — an authoritative account commands trust, and several can stand on the same shelf; only one can be definitive.

expert: Expert points at the credentials of the person — an expert opinion comes from mastery. Authoritative describes how the account itself is received: others defer to it and build on it, whoever wrote it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dubious: inviting doubt rather than trust

unreliable: not to be leaned on; liable to be wrong

Where it sits · how much weight the account carries with others

credible → authoritative → definitive

credible vs. authoritative: Credible is milder than authoritative: a credible report clears the bar of belief, while an authoritative one commands deference — others cite it and build on it.

definitive vs. authoritative: Definitive goes further than authoritative: several authoritative accounts can share a shelf, each trusted and weighty, but the definitive one is the last word, after which the debate closes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — author: originator, one who stands behind a thing (Latin auctor, from augēre, 'to increase, to make grow')

Suffix — -itative: carrying the quality of

Put it together: Auctor was Rome's word for the one who originates a thing and stands behind it — from augēre, 'to increase, to make grow' — and it gave English author. An authoritative account has a true auctor behind it: someone whose knowledge makes the work grow past what others managed, so that readers defer to it.

Use the root in a new word: augment: Night classes let her augment a salary that never quite stretched to the rent.

Root Check

Word Choice

measured / evaluative, approving

Authoritative praises a source: expert, weighty, deferred to. Do not let it shade into authoritarian, which condemns a ruler — the two share a root and almost nothing else in tone. An authoritative editor is trusted; an authoritarian one is merely obeyed. And age alone earns neither word: a first edition is only the earliest, not the one others defer to.
